text.p: Florida's Democratic governor Thursday let stand a bill passed by lawmakers that bans same-sex marriages and prohibits state agencies from recognising any marriage but that between a man and a woman.
Following the lead of other states and federal lawmakers, Gov. Lawton Chiles let a bill authorising the ban become law without his signature.
The law, which goes into effect immediately, allows state agencies to deny recognition of gay marriages regardless of where they took place.

"I believe that by and large most Floridians are tolerant and will one day come to view a broader range of domestic partnerships as an acceptable part of life," Chiles said in a statement defending his decision. "But, that is not the case today."

Florida law already restricts marriage to a man and a woman. Supporters of the ban, however, said if laws are passed in other states recognising gay marriages, the state would be powerless to prohibit it.
"This bill says that no other state or jurisdiction can change Florida policy," Chiles said. "It protects Florida's right to establish its own law about this important issue."

In 1996, President Clinton signed the "Defense of Marriage Act," a federal law that allows states to refuse to recognise marriage between partners of the same sex. In addition, the federal act defines marriage specifically as the union of one man and one woman.

The federal law came in response to a 1993 opinion by the Hawaii Supreme Court that ruled that gay couples could not be refused marriage licenses without violating the state constitution's ban against discrimination based on sexual orientation.
Opponents worried that the ruling would lead to a rush of homosexual couples to Hawaii to gain marital status and return home states to litigate rules in their resident states.
